title: Guardian POC weekly - observability, SSO & audit review
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on security/compliance checkpoints: SSO integration status, audit logs visibility, data retention defaults and SOC 2 alignment. Reviewed recent test results and agreed next steps for evidence collection and minor config changes for Redwood Private evaluation.
topics: pilot perf metrics and short tuning notes
next_steps: Redwood to share updated SSO SAML metadata and example IdP config (Maya) by 2025-08-22
Customer to run audit log ingestion test to Splunk and report results (Diego) by 2025-08-25

Redwood to provide SOC 2 control mapping doc and list of available evidence (Rae) by 2025-08-26
action_items: Maya - Send SSO metadata + step-by-step IdP guide - due 2025-08-22
Diego - Complete audit log forwarder test and share logs - due 2025-08-25
Jonah - Provision demo of Redwood Private with customer KMS integration - due 2025-08-29

questions: Does the audit log include token-level cost data or only request-level metadata?
Can retention be configured per-tenant and tied to the pilot agreement?

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-19
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Rae (Redwood CSM), Aisha (Head of Infra), Tom (Security Lead), Priya (PM), Diego (SRE)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — SSO status, audit logs/retention, SOC2 artifacts, plus any tuning notes from the last week's test run.
[00:18] Aisha: Yup, thanks. We only have 30 minutes on our side so if we can focus on the compliance bits first that would be great.
[00:24] Jonah: Totally. I'll start with a very short status of the POC infra and the logs we captured during the last 48h run. We saw about 3k requests, prefix cache hit rates around 18% before we enabled the KV cache tweak — after tweak it jumped to ~42%. Those numbers are just for reference, not the main ask today.
[00:40] Tom: Quick question, Jonah. For audit logs — what fields are you shipping by default? Are we getting userid, request payload hashes, model version, token counts, all of that?
[00:50] Jonah: Good q. Default runtime audit includes request_id, timestamp, model_id (sometimes transcribed as 'model name' in our logs), token_count, latency_ms, response_status. We also emit a user_id field if the request includes a mapped actor. We do not emit full request payload by default — that is opt-in because of PII concerns.
[01:12] Diego: Ok that sounds fine. We're pushing to Splunk; need a stable schema so our parsers don't break. Can you give sample log lines?
[01:20] Maya: I'll drop a log sample right after this call. I'll anonymize any PII.
[01:24] Aisha: On SSO — we started the IdP side. We tried to post the Redwood SAML metadata but our engineer hit an assertion error. Not sure if it's a metadata formatting mismatch or something on our end.
[01:36] Jonah: We see that sometimes. Different IdPs are fussy about the NameID format and AssertionConsumerService endpoints. Maya, I think we gave a newer metadata file last week — could be the older one.
[01:48] Maya: Yeah I'm looking at the demo tenant metadata — I probably sent the staging metadata. I'll regenerate the POC metadata (with the explicit ACS URL for the private control plane) and share it. Should fix the assertion issue.
[01:58] Priya: Is there a difference in SSO behavior between Hosted Redwood API vs Redwood Private? Our compliance team wants to understand whether SAML assertions are terminated in Redwood control plane or in their VPC for private deployments.
[02:10] Jonah: Short answer: For Hosted, the control plane handles assertion exchange and user mapping. For Redwood Private (customer-managed control plane) the assertions terminate inside customer-managed endpoints — effectively your IdP talks to your control plane endpoint. For the on-prem recipe we provide the SAML tooling you can host behind your SSO gateway.
[02:30] Tom: So for Private we get a much better security posture since assertions don't traverse Redwood's hosted control plane?
[02:35] Jonah: Correct, that's the preferred model for regulated workloads. There are configuration steps (metadata, certs, ACS URL) but functionally assertions stay within your boundary.
[02:42] Aisha: Good. SOC 2 folks asked whether audit logs are tamper-evident — can you sign logs or provide WORM retention?
[02:50] Rae: We don't provide WORM storage ourselves, but Redwood can forward logs to customer-controlled sinks (S3 with Object Lock, Splunk, SIEM) and we support signed log export in transit with TLS + mutual TLS for some add-ons. For evidence, we can show the forwarding configuration and delivery timestamps.
[03:10] Tom: Do you provide checksums or signing on each log line? We prefer a hash chain for higher assurance.
[03:16] Jonah: We currently don't offer per-log-line signed chains out of the box. It's something we discuss with larger customers — you can run a Lambda or Flink job on the receiving S3 bucket that computes a chain. We can demo an example pattern.
[03:28] Diego: That means we'll have to add a post-processor on our side. Fine, but we need sample code.
[03:33] Maya: I'll attach a reference snippet for Splunk and S3 with an example consumer that computes SHA256 and publishes an integrity document.
[03:41] Aisha: On data retention — what's default for pilot? We need to guarantee logs are kept for 90 days and inference results are purged after 30 days unless explicitly retained.
[03:50] Jonah: Default hosted retention is 30 days for runtime artifacts, 90 days for audit logs in the pilot plan can be configured. For Private you can set retention to whatever your policies require since it's customer-controlled storage. We can set retention rules and show the deletion lifecycle as evidence.
[04:06] Priya: Is there a per-tenant retention setting? We have a subset of data that is PII and we want shorter retention, everything else longer.
[04:13] Jonah: We support tenant-level retention policies in Dedicated and Private. Hosted can do workspace-level policies; tagging + routing can implement differential retention but it's a little more manual.
[04:24] Tom: Regarding SOC 2, what artifacts can you provide for common controls — user access reviews, change management, incident response?
[04:31] Rae: We maintain a SOC 2 report for our hosted controls and a control mapping doc that maps Redwood features to SOC 2 sections. For change management we can provide deployment logs, changelogs for the runtime (timestamps, author, rollout ID). For incident response we can share our incident policy and redacted postmortems where appropriate.
[04:48] Aisha: Will those artifacts be enough for our external auditor? They typically ask for evidence like change tickets linked to deployments.
[04:55] Rae: We can export the deployment audit trail and correlate with commit SHAs and PR numbers. For the POC we can provide redacted but linkable artifacts. For a full enterprise package we have a SOC 2 evidence portal as an add-on.
[05:07] Diego: One more small perf item from last week's run — we saw a 90ms tail latency spike on a rare path with long context (4k tokens). Any ideas on tuning?
[05:15] Jonah: That path is typically KV cache cold-start + kernel selection fallback. We can enable pre-warming for frequently used contexts and bump the continuous batching window slightly for that variant. There is a tradeoff with throughput but for POC it's fine.
[05:27] Priya: Let's avoid throughput tradeoffs unless necessary. We just want a stable 95th pct latency under 300ms.
[05:33] Jonah: Understood. We'll try the pre-warm + tuned batching and report next run.
[05:38] Maya: Quick operational question — how do we rotate keys if we integrate customer KMS for Private? Do you support HSM-backed keys and key rotation automation?
[05:46] Jonah: We integrate with customer KMS providers (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and you can bring your own keys. For HSM-backed keys you'd point to the provider's key ARN. Rotation is handled by the provider; Redwood will re-fetch the keys on rotation. We'll document the exact steps.
[05:59] Tom: Anything else from the security team?
[06:02] Aisha: One ask — can we get a short demo of the alerting/console so we can show the compliance team how audit searches work? They want to see live query of logs and export.
[06:11] Rae: Sure, Jonah can demo the Console. We'll schedule a 20-minute session for your compliance folks — morning slots next week are best for them.
[06:20] Maya: I'll propose times after this call.
[06:22] Priya: Also, small ask — do you have a document that maps logging fields to our compliance matrix? That'd make the auditor review easier.
[06:29] Rae: We do. I'll attach a field mapping doc and a sample Splunk dashboard template.
[06:34] Tom: On the SAML assertion error — one more detail: our IdP requires encrypted assertions using RSA-OAEP; does Redwood accept encrypted assertions or only signed?
[06:44] Jonah: We support signed assertions out of the box; encrypted assertions are supported in Private deployments where you control the endpoints. For Hosted, encrypted assertions are not currently supported in the standard flow.
[06:57] Aisha: That could be a blocker for Hosted, but not for Private. We'll escalate accordingly with our compliance folks.
[07:05] Maya: Recap and who's owning what: Maya sends SSO metadata and log samples; Jonah will prep a Private KMS demo and an example of log-forwarding + integrity script; Rae will send SOC2 mapping and field mappings; Diego will run Splunk ingestion test and share results. Any objections?
[07:20] Diego: Sounds good.
[07:22] Priya: Fine.
[07:24] Tom: No objections.
[07:26] Maya: OK great — last note: I'll include links to our security docs in the follow-up and the IdP troubleshooting checklist.
[07:32] Aisha: Appreciate it.
[07:34] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

Notes: occasional transcript noise: "Redwood Console" referred to as "the console" or "the shell" in places; "KV cache" sometimes transcribed as "K-V cache"; model names redacted by automated filter in the transcript.
